newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban blast Amnesty rights statement.
newsitem.headline: Taleban blast Amnesty rights statement.

text.p: A senior Taleban official on Monday criticised a statement from the human rights group Amnesty International and said he could no longer guarantee the security of Amnesty officials in Afghanistan.
An Amnesty statement issued last Friday accused the purist Moslem movement of arresting 2,000 people on ethnic grounds and demanded their immediate and unconditional release.

"The Amnesty report is completely baseless," said the Taleban's acting Interior Minister Mullah Kharullah Khairkhwa. "This report about the arrest of people in Kabul is the fault and propaganda of Amnesty International -- Amnesty International should be known as "The International Committee of Tyranny," he told journalists.
Khairkhwa denied Amnesty allegations that the prisoners were arrested on ethnic grounds and that they were kept in what were described as "apalling conditions".

"The information concerning the condition of the prisoners we have arrested is a lie. We have captured those who have been armed or the ones who have confessed that they are in the pay of (opposition leader Ahmed Shah) Masood." he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has also disputed the Amnesty numbers.

"The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) confirms that house searches and arrests have increased over the last two weeks, but based on our actual knowledge and current access to the major detention centres in Kabul, the number of people arrested for reasons linked to the conflict is substantially lower than those recently claimed in the international media," said Thomas Gurtner of the ICRC in Kabul on Sunday.
Khairkhwa did not know the exact number of prisoners being held, but said it was much lower than the number claimed by Amnesty.
"The number of prisoners taken recently is not known, but it should be around 100, not the 2,000 claimed by Amnesty," he said.

Khairkhwa said the Taleban would not be able to guarantee the security of Amnesty International or any other organisation which made similar accusations in the areas of Afghanistan controlled by the Taleban.
"I am interested to know who the people who report to Amnesty are, but may God not put them in my way." he said.

A spokesman for Amnesty defended the statement on Monday evening. He said Amnesty still believed that members of the Tajik and Hazara ethnic groups, from which the opposition draw the bulk of their support, were being singled out.

"The information we put out came from a number of reliable and independent sources. We do believe that people of Tajik and Hazara origin have been targetted recently." said the spokesman, speaking by telephone from London.
The spokesman said Amnesty was used to such threats.

"We have received threats in the past and we will continue to carry on the valuable work of highlighting human rights abuses and abusers. People who are interested in human rights would not make these kind of threats." said the spokesman.
